title: Distributed Systems & Concurrency
blurb: How real systems stay correct and available when spread across many machines that fail independently.
description: Replication, partitioning, consistency, availability, failure handling, and coordination -- how real systems stay correct at the scale distributed systems actually operate at. Practical and simulation-based.

lessons.title: Why distributed systems exist
objectives: Explain the real-world pressures that force a system to become distributed
Explain how scalability changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect scalability with fault tolerance and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A single machine has hard limits: it can only hold so much data, handle so many requests, and it's a single point of failure -- if it goes down, everything stops.
examples:
# the core trade-off, stated plainly:
# one machine: simple to reason about, but a single point of failure and a hard capacity ceiling
# many machines: can scale and survive failures, but now you must handle partial failure,
# network delays, and machines disagreeing about the current state -- for real
commonMistakes: Assuming distributed systems are 'better' by default -- they solve real problems, but at a real complexity cost; a single well-provisioned machine is often the RIGHT choice until you.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the foundational judgment call behind almost every real system-design interview question: does this problem actually need to be distributed, and if so, why?

lessons.title: Replication
objectives: Explain why systems replicate data and the trade-off between replication strategies
Explain how replication changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect replication with leader-based replication and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Replication means keeping copies of the same data on multiple machines -- for two reasons: durability (if one machine's disk dies, the data survives elsewhere) and availability (if one machine is down, another can still serve requests).
examples:
# the practical trade-off:
# synchronous replication: write returns only after replica confirms -- can't lose data,
#   but a slow/down replica slows down or blocks every write
# asynchronous replication: write returns immediately -- fast, but a leader crash
#   right after can lose the most recent writes that hadn't replicated yet
commonMistakes: Assuming replication alone guarantees no data loss -- asynchronous replication specifically trades a small window of potential data loss for speed; that's a deliberate, named trade-off, not.
lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every production database (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB) offers both modes -- knowing which to pick for which workload is a real, recurring backend decision.

lessons.title: Partitioning & consistent hashing
objectives: Explain why systems partition data and how consistent hashing minimizes reshuffling when nodes change
Explain how partitioning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect partitioning with sharding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Partitioning (sharding) splits data across multiple machines so no single machine has to hold or serve all of it -- each partition typically also gets replicated for durability.
examples:
# naive hashing's problem: hash(key) % 3 vs hash(key) % 4
# changes almost EVERY key's target node when the node count changes
#
# consistent hashing's fix: keys only move if they fall between
# the changed node's ring position and its neighbor -- a MINORITY of keys, not all
commonMistakes: Assuming naive modulo hashing is 'good enough' for a system that will ever add or remove nodes -- the reshuffling cost is exactly why consistent hashing exists as a named, widely-used.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is directly how real distributed caches (Memcached) and databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB) partition data -- and a common system-design interview building block.

lessons.title: The CAP theorem
objectives: Explain what CAP actually claims, and correct the most common misreading of it
Explain how CAP theorem changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CAP theorem with consistency and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The CAP theorem states that during a network partition (when some machines can't reach others), a distributed system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a response, even if it might be stale) -- it cannot guarantee both at the same time during that partition.
examples:
# during a network partition specifically:
# choose Consistency (CP): reject requests you can't verify are up-to-date -- correctness over uptime
# choose Availability (AP): answer anyway, possibly with stale data -- uptime over perfect correctness
# NOT during a partition: a good system can be both consistent AND available
commonMistakes: Treating CAP as 'pick 2 of 3, always' -- it's specifically about partition behavior; conflating it with a permanent, constant trade-off is the single most common misreading of this theorem.
lessons.careerRelevance: CAP is one of the most frequently cited (and frequently misquoted) concepts in system-design interviews -- being able to state it precisely is a genuine signal of real understanding.

# choose Consistency (CP): reject requests you can't verify are up-to-date -- correctness over uptime
# choose Availability (AP): answer anyway, possibly with stale data -- uptime over perfect correctness
# NOT during a partition: a good system can be both consistent AND available

lessons.title: Consistency models
objectives: Distinguish strong, eventual, and causal consistency by what guarantee each actually makes
Explain how strong consistency changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect strong consistency with eventual consistency and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Strong consistency guarantees every read sees the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data -- simplest to reason about, but requires coordination that costs latency.
examples:
# picking a consistency model by what actually breaks if it's wrong:
# bank balance -> needs strong consistency (a stale read could let you overdraw)
# view/like counter -> eventual consistency is fine (briefly stale count doesn't matter)
# comment thread replies -> causal consistency (a reply must appear AFTER the post it replies to)
commonMistakes: Assuming eventual consistency means 'eventually correct, so it's basically fine everywhere' -- for financial or safety-critical data, the WINDOW of staleness before convergence can cause.
lessons.careerRelevance: Real systems mix these deliberately -- e.g. a social media platform might use strong consistency for account balances/payments and eventual consistency for like counts, in the SAME product.
lessons.explain: Strong consistency guarantees every read sees the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data -- simplest to reason about, but requires coordination that costs latency.
lessons.example:

# view/like counter -> eventual consistency is fine (briefly stale count doesn't matter)

lessons.title: Availability & failure handling
objectives: Explain the difference between failing fast, failing gracefully, and failing silently -- and why the choice matters
Explain how fail fast changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect fail fast with graceful degradation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: In a distributed system, failure isn't an edge case -- it's a certainty that happens regularly (a machine dies, a network link drops, a disk fills up). Failing FAST means detecting a problem quickly and reporting it clearly, so the caller can react.
examples:
# graceful degradation example:
# recommendation service is down -> instead of erroring the whole page,
# show the page WITHOUT recommendations (a lesser experience, but the page still works)
# this beats both: crashing the whole request, AND silently showing an empty section
# with no logged error anywhere
commonMistakes: Silently catching and ignoring an exception 'to keep things running' -- this is one of the most common REAL causes of mysterious, hard-to-diagnose production bugs weeks later.
lessons.careerRelevance: Designing explicitly for HOW a component should fail (not just how it should succeed) is a hallmark of senior backend engineering judgment.

lessons.title: Idempotency
objectives: Explain why idempotency matters specifically because networks are unreliable
Explain how idempotency changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect idempotency with idempotency key and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An operation is idempotent if performing it multiple times has the exact same effect as performing it once. This matters enormously in distributed systems because networks are unreliable: a client might send a request, the server processes it successfully, but the RESPONSE gets lost -- the client, seeing no response, retries the exact same request.
examples:
# without an idempotency key: retry after a lost response -> customer charged TWICE
# with an idempotency key: server remembers request ID 'req-abc' was already processed ->
# a retry with the SAME ID returns the ORIGINAL result instead of charging again
commonMistakes: Assuming retries are automatically safe because 'the client will just get an error and stop' -- a LOST RESPONSE (not a lost request) is exactly the scenario where the server already.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every major payments API (Stripe, PayPal) requires an idempotency key on write operations specifically because of this -- a direct, practical, widely-tested pattern.

lessons.title: Retries, timeouts & circuit breakers
objectives: Explain why naive retries can make an outage worse, and how backoff and circuit breakers prevent that
Explain how exponential backoff changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect exponential backoff with circuit breaker and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Retrying a failed request seems obviously helpful, but retrying IMMEDIATELY and REPEATEDLY can make a struggling service's situation worse -- exactly when it's already overloaded, a flood of instant retries from every caller adds MORE load, not less.
examples:
# circuit breaker states:
# CLOSED (normal) -- failures accumulate -- threshold reached -> OPEN (reject immediately, no load added)
# OPEN -- after a cooldown timeout -> HALF-OPEN (allow ONE test request through)
# HALF-OPEN: succeeds -> CLOSED (back to normal). fails -> OPEN again (cooldown restarts)
commonMistakes: Retrying immediately in a tight loop with no backoff -- this is one of the most common REAL causes of a small outage turning into a much larger cascading failure across an entire system.
lessons.careerRelevance: Circuit breakers (Netflix's Hystrix popularized this pattern) are standard practice at any company operating microservices at scale -- directly relevant to backend and systems interview questions.

lessons.title: Leader election
objectives: Explain why some distributed operations need exactly one coordinator, and how nodes agree on who that is
Explain how leader election changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect leader election with split brain and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Some operations need exactly ONE node acting as the coordinator at any moment (e.g. deciding write order for a replicated log) -- having two nodes both believe they're the leader (a 'split brain') can cause serious inconsistency.
examples:
# simplified bully algorithm:
# node 2 notices the leader is down, and asks: is anyone with HIGHER priority still alive?
# if node 5 (highest) responds -> node 5 becomes leader
# if nodes 4 and 5 are BOTH down -> node 3 (next highest alive) becomes leader
# if node 2 gets no responses at all -> node 2 becomes leader itself
commonMistakes: Assuming leader election, once done, is permanent -- real systems must continuously detect leader failure and RE-elect, since the whole point is surviving the CURRENT leader eventually.
lessons.careerRelevance: Leader election underlies how real distributed databases (etcd, ZooKeeper-coordinated systems) maintain a single source of truth for cluster coordination.

lessons.title: Distributed locks
objectives: Explain what a distributed lock actually guards against, and why implementing one correctly is harder than it looks
Explain how distributed lock changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect distributed lock with lock expiry and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A distributed lock ensures only one node (or process) can perform a specific action at a time, even across machine boundaries -- e.g. preventing two servers from both processing the same scheduled job simultaneously.
examples:

# long enough that the lock EXPIRES
# node B acquires the lock (correctly, since it looks free)
# node A resumes, still THINKS it holds the lock -- now BOTH think they have it

lessons.title: Messaging & event-driven systems
objectives: Explain why decoupling services with a message queue changes failure behavior, not just architecture style
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: at-least-once delivery, at-most-once delivery, exactly-once semantics caveat, backpressure.
Explain how message queue changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect message queue with producer/consumer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: In a direct request/response call, if the receiving service is down, the request simply fails immediately. A message queue decouples this: the sender publishes a message and moves on; the queue holds it until a consumer is ready to process it -- meaning a temporarily-down consumer doesn't cause the sender to fail at all.
examples:
# direct call vs queue-based, when the downstream service is temporarily down:
# direct call: request fails immediately, caller must handle the error right now
# queue-based: message waits in the queue; once the consumer recovers, it processes
# the backlog -- the original caller never even knew there was a problem
commonMistakes: Assuming a message queue guarantees messages are processed in the exact order they were sent -- many real queue systems (for scalability reasons) only guarantee this per-partition/per-key.
lessons.careerRelevance: Kafka and RabbitMQ (the two most common real systems here) are directly asked about in backend and systems-design interviews at almost every company operating at meaningful scale. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Concurrency models & async programming
objectives: Distinguish concurrency at the distributed-systems level from single-machine threading, and explain why async I/O matters at scale
Explain how blocking I/O changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect blocking I/O with async/non-blocking I/O and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Within ONE machine handling MANY simultaneous distributed requests, blocking I/O (waiting synchronously for a network call or disk read to finish) wastes a thread that could otherwise be doing other work -- at scale, this severely limits how many concurrent connections a single machine can handle.
examples:
# blocking vs async, serving 10,000 concurrent slow network calls:
# blocking: needs (roughly) 10,000 threads, each stuck waiting -- huge memory/context-switch overhead
# async: a small pool of threads, each juggling many in-flight calls,
# resuming exactly when a result becomes ready -- vastly less overhead for the same load
commonMistakes: Assuming 'more threads' is the answer to handling more concurrent connections -- past a point, thread overhead itself becomes the bottleneck, which is exactly the problem async I/O is.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is precisely why Node.js, async Python (asyncio), and Go's goroutines are popular choices for high-concurrency backend services -- a direct, practical architecture decision.

lessons.title: Coordination
objectives: Explain what a coordination service actually provides, and why services build on it instead of solving these problems themselves
Explain how coordination service changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect coordination service with consensus protocol and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Distributed locks, leader election, and configuration management all require the SAME underlying capability: a small amount of data that many nodes can reliably agree on, even during failures.
examples:
# what teams build ON TOP of a coordination service, instead of reinventing:
# leader election -- 'who is currently the leader for this job?'
# distributed locks -- 'is this resource currently locked, and by whom?'
# service discovery -- 'which machines are currently healthy and serving this service?'
# configuration -- 'what's the current feature-flag value, consistently, everywhere?'
commonMistakes: Assuming every service should implement its own leader election or locking logic from scratch -- these are genuinely hard, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong problems, which is exactly why dedicated.

lessons.title: Distributed tracing basics
objectives: Explain why a single request spanning multiple services needs a shared trace ID to be debuggable at all
Explain how distributed tracing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect distributed tracing with trace ID and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A single user request in a microservices architecture might touch five, ten, or more services before a response is returned. Without any shared context, a slow or failing request is nearly impossible to debug -- each service's logs are separate, with no way to connect them into the story of ONE request's journey.
examples:
# without a trace ID: five separate services' logs, no way to connect them for one request
# with a trace ID: every service logs the SAME trace_id alongside its own work,
# letting you reconstruct: 'this exact request took 40ms in auth, then 300ms
# waiting on the database service, then 15ms formatting the response'
commonMistakes: Assuming individual service logs are enough to debug a slow multi-service request -- without a shared trace ID connecting them, there's no way to reconstruct which service's slowness.
lessons.careerRelevance: Distributed tracing (via tools like Jaeger or Zipkin) is considered baseline infrastructure at any company running more than a handful of microservices.

lessons.title: Designing for failure
objectives: Synthesize the course's ideas into a single design mindset: assume failure will happen, and design for it explicitly
Explain how fault tolerance mindset changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect fault tolerance mindset with failure modes and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every idea in this course shares one underlying principle: in a distributed system, failure isn't a rare edge case to patch around later -- it's a certainty that must be designed for from the start. Replication assumes a machine WILL die.
examples:
# the reframe this whole course is building toward:
# NOT: 'how do I make this system work?'
# BUT: 'how do I make this system work correctly WHEN (not if) something fails?'
# every technique in this course -- replication, retries, circuit breakers, idempotency --
# is a specific answer to a specific way something fails
commonMistakes: Treating failure-handling as something to add 'later, if there's time' -- retrofitting resilience into a system designed only for the happy path is far harder than designing for failure from.
lessons.careerRelevance: This mindset -- explicitly reasoning about failure modes before writing code -- is exactly what distinguishes strong systems/backend engineers in both interviews and real production incidents.

lessons.title: Consensus fundamentals: Raft & Paxos
objectives: Explain why distributed systems need consensus and the high-level roles of leader election, log replication, and quorums
Explain how consensus changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect consensus with Raft and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Consensus lets a group of machines agree on ordered state changes even when some machines or messages fail. Raft presents the problem through leader election, replicated logs, and majority commitment; Paxos is a foundational family of consensus algorithms with a different formulation.
lessons.example: Raft intuition: a leader appends a command to its log, replicates it to followers, and considers it committed after a majority acknowledges it. If the leader fails, a later election chooses a new leader that must preserve committed history.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

lessons.title: Distributed storage: replication & erasure coding
objectives: Compare full replication with erasure coding for durability, storage cost, and recovery
Explain how replication changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect replication with erasure coding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Replication stores full copies on multiple nodes, making reads and recovery straightforward but multiplying storage cost. Erasure coding splits data into fragments plus parity so the original can be reconstructed after some fragment loss with lower storage overhead, at the cost of more CPU/network work and more complex recovery.
lessons.example: Three-way replication stores roughly three full copies. An erasure-coded scheme can tolerate failures with less than 3x raw storage, but rebuilding a lost fragment may require reading several surviving fragments and computing reconstruction data.

It's against best practice for no specific reason

quiz.q: What does idempotency guarantee?
options: Performing an operation multiple times has the same effect as performing it once

quiz.q: Why do payment APIs require an idempotency key?
options: So a retried request (after a lost response) doesn't charge a customer twice
It's a legal requirement unrelated to retries

quiz.q: Why can immediate, repeated retries make an outage worse?
options: A flood of instant retries adds MORE load to an already-struggling service
Retries always fix the problem instantly

quiz.q: What does a circuit breaker do when it enters the OPEN state?
options: Sends even more requests to test recovery
Rejects requests immediately without adding load to the struggling service

quiz.q: What is a 'split brain' scenario in leader election?
options: Two nodes both believing they are the current leader simultaneously
A database running out of disk space

quiz.q: What makes implementing a distributed lock harder than an in-process lock?
options: Handling a node crashing while holding the lock, and clock differences between machines

quiz.q: How does a message queue change failure behavior compared to a direct call?
options: A temporarily-down consumer doesn't cause the sender to fail; the message waits in the queue
Queues make systems slower with no benefit

quiz.q: What ordering guarantee do many real message queues actually provide?
options: Global ordering across all messages always
Often only per-partition/per-key ordering, not global

quiz.q: Why does async/non-blocking I/O help handle more concurrent connections on one machine?
options: It uses more threads per connection
A small pool of threads can juggle many in-flight operations instead of one blocked thread per connection
It only works for reads, not writes

quiz.q: What do coordination services like ZooKeeper or etcd primarily provide?
options: A reliable way for many nodes to agree on a small amount of shared data, even during failures

quiz.q: Why is a shared trace ID essential for debugging a multi-service request?
options: Without it, there's no way to connect separate services' logs into one request's timeline

quiz.q: What is the core mindset this course argues distributed-systems design requires?
options: Assume failure will happen and design explicitly for how the system should behave when it does

exercises.title: Choose a replication mode
exercises.prompt: A system logs analytics events where losing the last few seconds of data during a crash is acceptable, but write speed matters a lot. Would you choose synchronous or asynchronous replication, and why?
exercises.hint: asynchronous -- the acceptable data-loss window trades for meaningfully faster writes, which matches this workload's priorities

exercises.title: Trace a consistent-hashing reassignment
exercises.prompt: Given a hash ring with nodes at positions 50, 150, 250, and keys hashing to 30, 90, 200, 280 -- which node does each key map to (clockwise, wrapping around)? If a new node is added at position 100, which keys actually move?
exercises.hint: only keys between 50 and 100 (the new node's position) reassign from node-150 to node-100 -- everything else stays exactly where it was

exercises.title: Identify the CAP misreading
exercises.prompt: A colleague says "our system can't be both consistent and available, ever, because of CAP." What's wrong with this statement?
exercises.hint: CAP's trade-off only applies DURING a network partition -- when the network is healthy, a well-designed system can offer both consistency and availability

exercises.title: Pick the right consistency model
exercises.prompt: For a live view-counter on a video (shown publicly, briefly stale is fine) versus an account balance (must never show a stale, too-high number a user could act on) -- which consistency model fits each?
exercises.hint: view counter: eventual consistency is fine. Account balance: needs strong consistency, since a stale read could let a user overdraw

exercises.title: Diagnose a silent failure
exercises.prompt: A service wraps every downstream call in a try/except that logs nothing and returns a default value on any error. Weeks later, a critical downstream outage went completely unnoticed. What's the actual root cause here, and what should change?
exercises.hint: the silent catch-and-ignore itself is the root cause -- it should log the error clearly (and likely alert) even while still returning a safe default, rather than hiding the failure entirely

exercises.title: Design an idempotency key
exercises.prompt: A client submits an order twice due to a lost response (same order, retried). What would you use as the idempotency key, and where should the server check it before processing?
exercises.hint: a client-generated unique ID sent with the request (e.g. a UUID); the server checks it BEFORE processing, and if already seen, returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate order

exercises.title: Trace exponential backoff
exercises.prompt: With base_delay=1 and doubling each retry, what are the wait times before attempts 2, 3, and 4?
exercises.hint: 1, 2, 4 -- doubling from the base delay each time

exercises.title: Trace a circuit breaker's states
exercises.prompt: A circuit breaker has failure_threshold=2. It sees: fail, fail, (circuit opens), a request comes in immediately after (before the cooldown), then after the cooldown a test request succeeds. What state is the circuit in after each event?
exercises.hint: CLOSED, CLOSED->OPEN (2nd failure hits threshold), still OPEN (rejected, cooldown not done), HALF-OPEN then CLOSED (test request succeeds)

exercises.title: Diagnose a split-brain risk
exercises.prompt: A leader-elected system re-elects a new leader after 5 seconds of no heartbeat, but the old leader (just slow, not actually dead) resumes normal operation 6 seconds later, unaware a new leader was elected. What's the risk, and what should the system check before acting as leader again?
exercises.hint: both nodes might now believe they're the leader (split brain); the old leader should check whether a newer leader term/epoch exists before resuming leader actions, and step down if so

exercises.title: Diagnose a distributed lock bug
exercises.prompt: Node A acquires a distributed lock with a 10-second expiry, then pauses (garbage collection) for 15 seconds. What happens to the lock, and what's the resulting risk?
exercises.hint: the lock expires while node A is paused; another node can correctly acquire it; when node A resumes, it still believes it holds the lock -- now two nodes both think they have exclusive access

exercises.title: Choose direct call or message queue
exercises.prompt: A checkout flow needs to send a confirmation email after payment succeeds. Should this be a direct synchronous call, or published to a queue? Why?
exercises.hint: a queue -- the email service being temporarily down shouldn't fail or delay the actual checkout; the message can wait in the queue and be sent once the email service recovers

exercises.title: Explain a message-ordering gotcha
exercises.prompt: A team assumes their message queue delivers all messages in the exact order they were published, globally. What's the likely gap in this assumption, and how would you verify it for their specific queue?
exercises.hint: most real queues (for scalability) only guarantee ordering per-partition/per-key, not globally across all partitions -- check the specific queue's documentation and partition/key strategy

exercises.title: Explain async I/O's benefit at scale
exercises.prompt: A service needs to handle 5,000 concurrent slow network calls. Explain, in your own words, why a small thread pool with async I/O handles this better than one thread per connection.
exercises.hint: one-thread-per-connection means 5,000 threads mostly sitting idle waiting, with real memory/context-switching overhead; async I/O lets a small number of threads juggle many in-flight operations, resuming each only when its result is ready

exercises.title: Decide whether to use a coordination service
exercises.prompt: A team is about to hand-write their own leader-election logic from scratch for a new service. What would you ask them before they start, and what would you suggest instead?
exercises.hint: ask whether they've considered using an existing coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul) instead -- leader election is a genuinely hard, easy-to-get-wrong problem that's already been solved and heavily tested elsewhere

exercises.title: Explain why a trace ID matters
exercises.prompt: A request is slow, and it touched 6 different microservices. Without a shared trace ID, why is this hard to debug -- and what does the trace ID actually fix?
exercises.hint: each service's logs are separate with no way to connect them into one request's story; a shared trace ID logged by every service lets you reconstruct exactly which service in the chain caused the delay

exercises.title: Apply the failure-first mindset
exercises.prompt: You're designing a new service that calls two downstream APIs. Before writing the happy-path code, list at least 3 concrete failure modes you should design for first.
exercises.hint: examples: either downstream API times out or errors (need retries/circuit breakers), a request gets duplicated by a client retry (need idempotency), one downstream API is slow but not failed (need a sane timeout so it doesn't block everything)

exercises.title: Diagnose an availability vs consistency choice
exercises.prompt: During a network partition, a shopping cart service chooses to keep accepting adds-to-cart on every node, resolving conflicts later, rather than rejecting requests it can't verify are consistent. Which side of the CAP trade-off did it choose, and is that a reasonable choice for a shopping cart specifically?
exercises.hint: it chose availability (AP) over strict consistency; reasonable for a shopping cart, since a temporarily-inconsistent cart that gets reconciled later is a much smaller problem than rejecting a user's ability to add items during a partition

exercises.title: Combine idempotency with retries
exercises.prompt: A client uses exponential backoff to retry a failed payment request up to 4 times. Without an idempotency key, what could go wrong even with well-designed backoff?
exercises.hint: backoff controls WHEN retries happen, not WHETHER they're safe -- without an idempotency key, if an earlier attempt actually succeeded server-side but the response was lost, a well-spaced retry can still duplicate the charge

projects.title: Consistent hash ring simulator
projects.desc: Build a simulator showing key-to-node assignment on a hash ring, and demonstrate that adding/removing a node reassigns only a minority of keys.

projects.title: Retry-and-circuit-breaker client wrapper
projects.desc: Wrap an unreliable (simulated) API call with exponential backoff and a circuit breaker, demonstrating all three circuit states under sustained failure and recovery.

projects.title: Idempotent request processor
projects.desc: Build a request handler that deduplicates retried requests using an idempotency key, with a test suite proving duplicate requests never double-process.

projects.title: Simplified leader election simulator
projects.desc: Implement the bully algorithm across a set of simulated nodes, correctly handling leader failure and re-election.

projects.title: Event-driven order pipeline (simulated)
projects.desc: Design a simulated order-processing pipeline where services communicate via published events rather than direct calls, demonstrating that a temporarily-down consumer doesn't block the producer.

interviewPreparation.q: Explain the CAP theorem precisely -- what exactly does it claim, and what's the most common way people misstate it?
interviewPreparation.a: During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response, even if possibly stale) -- it can't guarantee both simultaneously during that partition. The most common misreading treats this as a permanent, all-the-time trade-off, when it specifically only applies during partition conditions; a well-designed system can offer both when the network is healthy.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does an idempotency key matter for a payment API specifically?
interviewPreparation.a: Networks can lose a response even after the server successfully processed a request. Without an idempotency key, a client's retry (believing the original attempt failed) would cause the server to process the same payment a second time. The idempotency key lets the server recognize the retry and return the original result instead of duplicating the charge.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk through what a circuit breaker does and why immediate, unlimited retries can make an outage worse.
interviewPreparation.a: A circuit breaker tracks consecutive failures; once a threshold is hit, it moves to OPEN and rejects requests immediately without adding more load to the struggling downstream service, then cautiously tests recovery via a HALF-OPEN state before fully resuming. Without this, every caller retrying immediately and repeatedly floods an already-overloaded service with even more traffic, which can turn a partial slowdown into a full outage.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is consistent hashing preferred over naive hash(key) % N partitioning in a system that will scale up or down?
interviewPreparation.a: Naive modulo hashing reassigns almost every key when the node count changes, since the modulo result shifts for nearly all keys. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a conceptual ring, so adding or removing a node only reassigns the keys between it and its neighbor -- a minority of keys, not nearly all of them.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between a message queue and a direct API call, in terms of failure behavior?
interviewPreparation.a: A direct call fails immediately if the receiving service is down. A message queue decouples the two -- the message waits in the queue until a consumer is available, meaning a temporarily-down consumer doesn't cause the sender to fail at all, at the cost of not getting an immediate confirmation that the work is fully done.

capstone.title: Design and Simulate a Fault-Tolerant Distributed Service
capstone.description: Design a small distributed service (e.g. a simplified order-processing system) that explicitly handles replication, partitioning, retries with backoff, a circuit breaker, idempotent request handling, and leader election for a coordinator role -- then simulate at least 3 realistic failure scenarios and show the system behaving correctly (or explain precisely what it sacrifices and why).
deliverables: An architecture diagram showing replication, partitioning strategy, and where a coordinator/leader role is needed

A working simulation of at least 3 failure scenarios: a node failure requiring leader re-election, a downstream service becoming unavailable (triggering circuit-breaker behavior), and a duplicated client request (proving idempotent handling)
A written explanation of which consistency model was chosen for which piece of data, and why -- tied to CAP trade-offs specific to this system
Test cases proving idempotent handling actually prevents duplicate processing
A short section explicitly stating what this design deliberately sacrifices (e.g. some staleness window, or added latency) and why that trade-off was chosen
capstone.portfolioTips: Explicitly stating what your design SACRIFICES (not just what it achieves) is exactly the kind of trade-off-aware thinking senior system-design interviews are testing for -- most candidates only describe the happy path.

industryUsage.usage: DynamoDB uses consistent hashing for partitioning and offers tunable consistency (strong or eventual) per request -- a direct, production example of nearly every concept in this course.
Popularized the circuit-breaker pattern (via their Hystrix library) specifically to prevent cascading failures across their large microservices architecture.
Requires an idempotency key on payment-creation API calls specifically to make retries after a lost response safe -- one of the clearest real-world idempotency examples in production use.

careerApplications: Used by backend, platform, cloud, and infrastructure engineers to design reliable services across multiple machines, including replication, consistency, coordination, retries, queues, and failure handling.
